nodes.title: Revisions
nodes.body:
04/14/89.  Thomas Czapla; NOAA SEA Division

FLELMR CODE: 5198

nodes.title: Kingdom Animalia
nodes.body:
Phylum: Mollusca
      Class: Bivalvia
      Order: Veneroida
      Family: Mactridae

Note: Subclass Heterodonta (Neumayr, 1884); Superfamily Mactroidea (Lamarck, 1809)
Common Name: Common Rangia

Other Common Names: Atlantic rangia, Marsh clam (81); brackish water clam, road clam, wedge clam.

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial: The commercial value of this clam lies in the use of its shell in the manufacture of cement, glass, chemicals chicken and cattle feed, wallboard and other building products, agricultural lime, road construction and as fill in nearshore oil exploration (711). This clam is used for blue crab bait and some human consumption (239 401).

Indicator: Rangia is a commonly used bivalve for tests of toxicity, bioaccumulation and pollutant concentrations in tissues of petroleum products and by-products (491 209 369 45) and heavy metals (426).

Ecological Role: These clams are linked to primary producers and secondary consumers in estuarine areas, because they convert detritus into biomass which can be utilized by many fishes and crustaceans (341 89 401).

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall: Although there is an extended range for this species in the geologic record, present day ranges are limited to the Atlantic coast around the Chesapeake Bay region; southwestern Florida to Texas and to Alvarado, Veracruz, Mexico (14 239).

Within Study Area: From the Corpus Christi Bay area to Mobile Bay; concentrated in brackish waters of Louisiana.

Mobility and Migration:
Larvae are presumed to be negatively phototrophic and are expected to be associated near the bottom of shallow bay margins.
Juveniles and adults are sedentary with only the posterior end and siphons slightly exposed. Laboratory held specimens would only move toward the sediment surface when covered by sand. Attached organisms (barnacles, mussels and algae) indicate a stationary position for long periods of time (207). Because of the clams small mass they can be easily buffeted about by shifting water currents (401) .

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body: Little is known of the early natural life modes but eggs and larvae are predicted to have a limited pelagic existence (207). Juveniles and adults are sedentary benthic infauna with only a limited portion of the shell protruding from the sediment in brackish and estuarine waters. Juveniles and adults are generally restricted to shallower water along bay margins, presumably due to the concentration of free-swimming larvae by wave action where the metamorphosis to a benthic existence occurs.

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body: Habitat Type: The common rangia is found in river-influenced brackish water (riverine-oligohaline). The clam which prefers a combination of low salinity, high turbidity and a substrate of sand, mud and vegetation (401).

nodes.title: Substrate
nodes.body: There is a trend for larger sized Rangia to inhabit sandy bottom areas, suggesting larger sized particles trap more food, sandy substrates facilitate burrowing and excretory products do not accumulate (711). In the Trinity River delta, Texas, rangia is found in soft mud-clay-silt substrates (27). The sediments that Rangia resides in can result in shell erosion and ultimate mortality because of presence of acids formed in the breakdown of detritus. Fairbanks (207) noted the massive amount of shell erosion in the north shore is of Lake Pontchartrain due to the presence of carbonic acids, produced from carbon dioxide reacting with high concentrations of organic matter.

nodes.title: Physical/chemical
nodes.body:
Temperature: Optimum condition for embryos is 18-29 C. The planktonic existence is of larvae is greatly extended by low temperatures, larvae survive 8-32 C, growth is best at 20-32 C 401).

Salinity: Clams can tolerate a wide range of salinities, generally from 0-25 ppt, osmoregulating with inorganic and intracellular free amino acids to control cell volumes (527). Spawning, becomes physiologically impossible if salinities are < 1 or >15 ppt for long periods. Optimal salinities for embryos range 6-10 ppt; larvae survive 2-20 ppt; and growth is best at 10-20 ppt (401).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode: Fertilization is external, gametes are released directly into the water.

Spawning Strategy: Fairbanks (207) identified two distinct periods of spawning per year; a spring spawn (March-May) and a less intense period from late summer to November. In most area rangia spawn from March to May and late summer to November but it may be continuous from March to November. Wolfe and Petteway (773) found spawning to occur from July to November with a peak in September.

Fecundity: No fecundity data is available.

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg: Eggs (69 u) fertilized in the laboratory took approximately 26 h to develop into pelagic trochophore larvae at 73-80 F.

Larvae: Trochophore larvae developed to veliger stage (93 u) in 8 h. Larval period is dependent on temperature and food, but generally is short lived. These stages are extremely fragile and may not be picked up in normal sampling efforts.

Juvenile: The minimum size of settling spat is approximately 375 u. Growth of juveniles is 15-20 mm in the first year, 5-9 in the second and 4-5 in the third year (207). Suspended solids above the substratum significantly inhibit the growth of rangia compared to the substrate itself (207).

Adult: Rangia around the size of 24 mm are considered sexually mature, being reached in 2-3 years (207).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Food of the common rangia consists of diatoms, algae and detritus, with detritus comprising the greatest portion. Rangia is a filter feeder, controlling the food movements with the gill palps and ciliary currents over the gills (401).

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body: This species appears to be important to the diet of the migratory lesser scaup duck Aythya affinis and may be replaced in their diet under more saline conditions by the clam Mulinia lateralis (711). Sixteen species of fishes (Dasyatis sabina, Lepisosteus productus, L. spatula, L. osseus, Dorosoma cepedianum, Anchoa mitchilli, Arius felis, Ictalurus furcatus, Aplodinotus grunniens, Leiostomus xanthurus, Micropogon undulatus, Pogonias cromis, Archosargus oviceps, Lagodon rhomboides, Paralichthys lethostigma, Cynoscion arenarius) and five invertebrates (Penaeus setiferus, Macrobrachium ohione, Callinectes sapidus, Rhithropanopeus harrisii, and Thais haemostoma) have been reported to consume Rangia (711). Sporocysts and cercarial larvae have been described from rangia in Galveston Bay, Texas (757); sporocysts cause castration in the clam.
